questions.prompt: How does this chapter define directness?
choices: Practicing in the real context of the target skill
Studying a skill from as many books as possible
Skipping all preparation and starting cold

explanation.gentle: Directness means moving practice into the context where the skill will actually have to work.
explanation.direct: A is correct because the chapter defines directness through target-context practice, not through quantity of study or reckless immediacy.
explanation.competitive: The chapter wants arena contact, not blind jumping or endless reading.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter care so much about directness?
choices: Because transfer is not automatic
Because realistic practice is always easier
Because scaffolding is never useful

explanation.gentle: Young argues that improvement does not automatically carry from one setting into another.
explanation.direct: A captures the chapter's transfer logic: practice has to resemble the target context more closely if the skill is going to carry over well.
explanation.competitive: Skills do not migrate generously from tidy prep to the real fight.

questions.prompt: Nadia wants to do stronger client-style work but has mostly been reading frameworks. What move best follows the chapter?
choices: Replace part of the reading with target-like client problems
Keep reading until the knowledge feels complete
Avoid realistic tasks until confidence is perfect

explanation.gentle: The chapter would move her practice closer to the kind of problem-solving the real role requires.
explanation.direct: A follows directness by reducing the gap between preparation and the target context.
explanation.competitive: Start solving the kind of problem that will eventually judge the skill.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of a comfortable proxy?
choices: It can weaken transfer by removing the real task conditions
It always teaches nothing at all
It makes the learner morally lazy

explanation.gentle: The chapter warns that a clean proxy can omit the exact pressures and constraints that later matter most.
explanation.direct: A is correct because the danger is not zero learning. It is learning that carries poorly into the real arena.
explanation.competitive: A flattering substitute can train the wrong performance.

questions.prompt: Leo rehearses well at home but feels unstable in the real presentation room. What does that suggest?
choices: His practice has lacked enough directness
He needs more note-taking
He should avoid the room until he feels calmer

explanation.gentle: The change in room shows that the environment itself is part of the skill challenge.
explanation.direct: A fits the chapter because the rehearsal context has been too far from the real performance context.
explanation.competitive: He trained in comfort and got surprised by the arena.

questions.prompt: What limit does the chapter place on directness?
choices: The most realistic version must always happen immediately
Scaffolding can help if it leads toward target contact
Indirect work should be permanent for complex skills

explanation.gentle: Young allows staged increases in directness when they act as bridges toward the real task.
explanation.direct: B states the chapter's boundary: scaffolds are allowed, but only if they reduce the distance to the target context.

questions.prompt: Talia must choose between a polished proxy rehearsal and a messier target-like rehearsal. Which choice matches the chapter?
choices: Choose the version that preserves more of the real event conditions
Choose the cleaner one because confidence matters more than transfer
Avoid both until she understands the theory better

explanation.gentle: The chapter prefers practice that better matches the real performance context.
explanation.direct: A follows directness by valuing transfer over comfort.
explanation.competitive: Pick the rehearsal that judges by the right standards.

questions.prompt: When does a scaffold stop helping and start sheltering the learner?
choices: When it stops reducing the distance to the target context
When it is repeated more than once
When it feels a little uncomfortable

explanation.gentle: The chapter judges scaffolds by direction: do they still move practice toward the real arena?
explanation.direct: A is right because the problem begins when the scaffold becomes a permanent substitute instead of a bridge.
explanation.competitive: The bridge becomes a bunker when forward motion stops.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter treat real-context practice as more revealing?
choices: Because the target arena answers back more honestly
Because realistic practice always feels easier
Because indirect work has no value at any stage

explanation.gentle: The chapter says the real arena exposes what still feels unstable or unfamiliar more clearly.
explanation.direct: A fits the principle because directness reveals transfer weaknesses that proxies can hide.
explanation.competitive: The harsh verdict is useful because it is honest.

questions.prompt: If practice is finally aimed at the right arena, what question naturally comes next?
choices: Which weak point inside the performance should be isolated and drilled
How to make the proxy even cleaner
How to avoid discomfort during realistic practice

explanation.gentle: Once the learner is practicing in the right context, the next useful question is which part is still weakest.
explanation.direct: A is the right bridge because drill becomes meaningful only after directness improves.
explanation.competitive: After the field is right, hunt the weakest link.
